strengths: Clear identification of spurious correlation problem with compelling empirical evidence (gradient saliency maps showing MLLMs attend more to backgrounds than LLMs)
Well-motivated causal framework using SCMs to distinguish causal factors (Lc) from spurious factors (Ls)
Novel token-level causal completeness reward combining sufficiency and necessity constraints
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (4 architectures) and diverse benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, GPT-4, high-resolution, grounding, mathematical reasoning)
Consistent improvements across settings and compatibility with multiple GRPO variants (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, GCPO)
Good presentation with effective visualizations and clear pseudo-code for reproducibility
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating importance of sufficiency and necessity components
Extensive supplementary material with additional experiments and detailed implementation information
weaknesses: Causal reward formulation (Eq. 8) appears ad-hoc without justification for linear combination over alternatives; Definition 3.1 lacks clarity on why sufficiency and necessity components are combined this way

Approximations in causal estimation not thoroughly analyzed: Eq. 6 uses masking with H forward passes and Eq. 7 uses simple masking to approximate counterfactuals; accuracy compared to true causal intervention unclear

Modest marginal improvements on several benchmarks (POPE F1 typically +0.8-1.5 points, often within potential noise margins); improvements over GCPO are small despite GCPO already incorporating causal reasoning
Computational overhead of causal rewards (multiple forward passes per token) not quantified in absolute terms; Figure 12 shows relative efficiency but absolute cost unclear
Limited mechanistic analysis of why causal token rewards prevent background-driven hallucinations; deeper explanation of the connection between method and outcome would strengthen claims
Experiments limited to models ≤7B parameters; paper acknowledges not testing on 72B+ models, limiting assessment of scalability and generalizability

Non-differentiable indicator function in Eq. 6 could affect gradient-based training but this isn't discussed; negligible difference between applying rewards to all tokens vs. reasoning tokens suggests design choice may not be critical
Limited guidance on hyperparameter selection (λs, λn, H) for new domains; evaluation predominantly on COCO-derived variants without out-of-distribution testing
No statistical significance testing despite modest effect sizes; GPT-4 evaluation has inherent biases and limited ground truth
Missing discussion of failure modes and hallucination types the method doesn't address; unclear why linear combination is appropriate for integrating sufficiency and necessity
